stages.title: See what Listen Out does and how a round plays

screens.title: Look at a round of Listen Out, from the first sound to the score

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you will know how a round of Listen Out plays and how it scores.
Listen Out is a listening game. It is on Slieve Donard, the last and highest place on the Summit Ready map.
You build one game from each pair of game chapters. Listen Out is paired with Route Timer, so you build one of those two.
First you build Listen Out exactly as it is in Summit Ready. Then, in stage 5, you change it into a listening game on your own topic.
In Listen Out, the question is a sound and the answers are pictures. Each sound is a [[sound file|0]] that plays when you press **Play the sound**.
Under the button are 4 pictures, each with a name, such as Red grouse or Rescue helicopter. One of the 4 pictures made the sound.
The 4 pictures stay grey until you have played the sound once. You have to listen before you guess.

screenshot.alt: Listen Out at the start of a round, with Play the sound and 4 grey pictures
screenshot.cap: The start of a round. The 4 pictures stay grey until you press Play the sound.

blocks.p: You can play each sound 3 times. The sentence beside the button counts down your plays. After the third play, the button turns grey and does nothing.
Click the picture that made the sound. The right picture turns green. If you picked a different picture, your picture turns red.
The box under the pictures then says what made the sound, and one fact about it.

screenshot.cap: After a right answer: the picture is green, Points goes up by 10, and Next sound appears.

blocks.p: A round is 10 sounds. Each right answer is worth 10 points, so the best score is 100 points.
After the 10th sound, the button says **See my score**. It opens the Round over box, and the flag on Slieve Donard gets a tick on the map.

words: sound file
A file that holds a sound. Summit Ready's sounds are .wav files in the Sounds folder.
bin\Debug
The folder inside your project where Visual Studio 2019 puts the program it builds. Summit Ready reads its data, pictures and sounds from there.
zip file
One file with other files and folders packed inside it.
property
A named value that an object carries, such as `Name` on a ListenClip. `{ get; set; }` lets other code read the value and change it.
constructor
A method with the same name as its class. It runs once, when code makes a new object with `new`.
static
A method marked `static` belongs to the class itself. You call it on the class name, as in `ListenClip.LoadAll()`.
List
A list that grows as you add to it. `List<ListenClip>` is a list that holds ListenClip objects.
continue
Inside a loop, `continue` skips the rest of this turn of the loop. The loop goes straight on to its next turn.
not
`!` in front of a true or false value turns it the other way. `!answered` is true while `answered` is false.
lightning bolt
The button at the top of the Properties window that shows a control's events in place of its properties.
panel
A control that holds other controls. `pnlPlay` is the play area that holds the button and the 4 pictures.
field
A variable written at the top of the class, outside every method. Every method in the form can use it, and it keeps its value until the window closes.
array
A row of values of the same type, kept together under one name and numbered from 0. `picks[0]` is the first picture button, and `picks[3]` is the 4th.
random number
`random.Next(13)` gives a whole number picked by chance, from 0 up to 12.
Contains
`choices.Contains(n)` is true when the list `choices` already holds `n`.
null
`null` means no object at all. `Files.Picture` gives back `null` when the picture file is missing.
Bitmap
A picture held in memory. `new Bitmap(photo, 210, 180)` makes a copy of `photo` that is 210 pixels wide and 180 pixels tall.
colour from red, green and blue
`Color.FromArgb(62, 142, 65)` mixes a colour from red, green and blue. Each number is from 0 to 255.
Cursor
The pointer the mouse shows over a control. `Cursors.Hand` is the pointing hand.
Enabled
When a control's Enabled is false, it turns grey and clicks on it do nothing.
take away 1
`playsLeft--` takes 1 away from `playsLeft`.
event
Something that happens to a control, such as a click on a button.
handler
The method that runs when an event happens. `Pick_Click` is the handler for a click on any of the 4 pictures.
sender
Every handler is given `sender`: the control that the event happened to, such as the picture that was clicked.
and
`&&` means and. The `if` is true only when both of its parts are true.
StartsWith
`"whistle-six".StartsWith("whistle")` is true, because the text starts with those letters.
quote mark inside text
Inside quotes, `\"` stands for one quote mark, so the quote mark shows on the screen and does not end the text.
AddRange
`AddRange` adds every line of one list to the end of another list.
red underline
The wavy red line Visual Studio 2019 draws under code it does not understand yet. Often it means a method you have not written yet.

blocks.p: By the end of this screen, you will know what each line of `listen.txt` holds.
Listen Out gets its sounds from a text file, `listen.txt`. The file is already in your bin\Debug\Data folder, because `summit-ready-files.zip` put it there in chapter 2.
The file has 13 sounds, and each round plays 10 of them, so a round is never quite the same twice.
You do not type `listen.txt`. You read it here, so that the code in stage 4 makes sense.

box.title: If a file is missing or broken

blocks.p: Listen Out never crashes because a file is missing. This is what you see instead.
If `listen.txt` is missing, or has fewer than 10 lines with 4 parts, **Play the sound** turns grey. The sentence beside it says **Listen Out needs 10 sounds in Data\listen.txt, each with 4 parts.**
If a line of `listen.txt` does not have exactly 4 parts, Listen Out skips that line.
If a picture is missing, its button shows only the name.
If a sound is missing, **Play the sound** is silent, and the game carries on.
To put a missing file back, you download the [[zip file|2]] again and paste its folders into bin\Debug. When Windows asks about the files you already have, you click **Skip these files**.
Skipping keeps every file you already have, including any file you changed. Only the missing files are copied in.

code.title: ListenClip.cs: the ListenClip class
code.why: You type the 4 properties, and the 4 lines that put a value into each one, because they are new. The rest reads a file the same way as `LoadAll` in chapter 3, so it comes in the copy.
partLines: The class and its 4 properties

`class ListenClip` starts the class. Each property holds one part of a line of `listen.txt`. `FileName` holds the file name with no ending, and `Name` holds the name under the picture. `InSentence` holds the name inside a sentence, and `Explanation` holds the fact. `{ get; set; }` lets other code read each property and change it.
The constructor

This part is the constructor. It runs when code writes `new ListenClip(parts)`. `parts` is one line of `listen.txt`, already cut into 4 pieces at each bar. The constructor puts `parts[0]` into `FileName`, and so on down to `parts[3]` in `Explanation`.
The start of LoadAll

`static` means that you call LoadAll on the class itself, as `ListenClip.LoadAll()`. You do not need a ListenClip object first. LoadAll starts with an empty list. `Files.Data` from chapter 2 gives the full path of `listen.txt` in the Data folder. `!` means not. If `listen.txt` is not there, LoadAll hands back the empty list, so the game shows a message and does not crash.
Read every line

The StreamReader is the part of C# that reads a file line by line. It opens `listen.txt`. The loop goes round once for each line, until the end of the file. `Split('|')` cuts each line at each bar into `parts`. If a line does not have exactly 4 parts, `continue` skips it and the loop moves on to the next line. Every line with 4 parts becomes a new ListenClip, and `clips.Add` puts it on the end of the list.
Close the file and hand back the list
`reader.Close()` closes `listen.txt`, so that other programs can open it again. `return clips;` hands the full list back to the code that called LoadAll.

code.title: The Listen Out fields
partLines: The sounds
`clips` holds every sound that LoadAll reads from `listen.txt`. `order` holds the sounds' numbers in a random order, so each round plays them in a new order.
This sound
`number` counts the sounds in this round, from 0 to 9. `playsLeft` is how many plays this sound has left. `answered` turns true once the player clicks a picture.

code.title: PickChoices and FindClip
partLines: Start with the right sound
PickChoices is given `answer`, the number of the sound that plays. The list `choices` starts with that number.
Keep the two whistles together
If the sound is one whistle, the other whistle goes into `choices` next. FindClip finds where that whistle is in the list.
3 more sounds, with no repeats

The loop goes round until `choices` holds 4 numbers. `random.Next(clips.Count)` gives a [[random number|13]] from 0 up to one less than the number of sounds. `!choices.Contains(n)` is true when `n` is not in the list yet, so a sound is never added twice.
FindClip
FindClip looks through every sound for the one called `fileName`, and gives back its place in the list. If no sound has that name, it gives back 0, so the game still has a picture to show.

glossary: sound file
A file that holds a sound. Summit Ready's sounds are .wav files in the Sounds folder.
bin\Debug
The folder inside your project where Visual Studio 2019 puts the program it builds. Summit Ready reads its data, pictures and sounds from there.
zip file
One file with other files and folders packed inside it.
property
A named value that an object carries, such as `Name` on a ListenClip. `{ get; set; }` lets other code read the value and change it.
constructor
A method with the same name as its class. It runs once, when code makes a new object with `new`.
static
A method marked `static` belongs to the class itself. You call it on the class name, as in `ListenClip.LoadAll()`.
List
A list that grows as you add to it. `List<ListenClip>` is a list that holds ListenClip objects.
continue
Inside a loop, `continue` skips the rest of this turn of the loop. The loop goes straight on to its next turn.
not
`!` in front of a true or false value turns it the other way. `!answered` is true while `answered` is false.
lightning bolt
The button at the top of the Properties window that shows a control's events in place of its properties.
panel
A control that holds other controls. `pnlPlay` is the play area that holds the button and the 4 pictures.
field
A variable written at the top of the class, outside every method. Every method in the form can use it, and it keeps its value until the window closes.
array
A row of values of the same type, kept together under one name and numbered from 0. `picks[0]` is the first picture button, and `picks[3]` is the 4th.
random number
`random.Next(13)` gives a whole number picked by chance, from 0 up to 12.
Contains
`choices.Contains(n)` is true when the list `choices` already holds `n`.
null
`null` means no object at all. `Files.Picture` gives back `null` when the picture file is missing.
Bitmap
A picture held in memory. `new Bitmap(photo, 210, 180)` makes a copy of `photo` that is 210 pixels wide and 180 pixels tall.
colour from red, green and blue
`Color.FromArgb(62, 142, 65)` mixes a colour from red, green and blue. Each number is from 0 to 255.
Cursor
The pointer the mouse shows over a control. `Cursors.Hand` is the pointing hand.
Enabled
When a control's Enabled is false, it turns grey and clicks on it do nothing.
take away 1
`playsLeft--` takes 1 away from `playsLeft`.
event
Something that happens to a control, such as a click on a button.
handler
The method that runs when an event happens. `Pick_Click` is the handler for a click on any of the 4 pictures.
sender
Every handler is given `sender`: the control that the event happened to, such as the picture that was clicked.
and
`&&` means and. The `if` is true only when both of its parts are true.
StartsWith
`"whistle-six".StartsWith("whistle")` is true, because the text starts with those letters.
quote mark inside text
Inside quotes, `\"` stands for one quote mark, so the quote mark shows on the screen and does not end the text.
AddRange
`AddRange` adds every line of one list to the end of another list.
red underline
The wavy red line Visual Studio 2019 draws under code it does not understand yet. Often it means a method you have not written yet.
